I’ll check the verifier’s power spectrum on F1 during the elevated-energy period for a training-like periodic line.

steps.think: Competing explanations: (H1) Honest: no run exceeded 50,000 GPU-hours; records consistent. Check: inventory vs system_list, utility_energy vs scheduler-implied power, balance_checks. (H2) Honest but messy: lost logs or late payments cause gaps that look suspicious. Check: log_escrow vs scheduler_log, bank_payments, customer_check on the register. (H3) Split run: one large training run labelled as several smaller jobs or customers (possibly shell customers the operator controls). Check: customer_check register entries, interconnect_tap on A-B for cross-cluster training traffic, power_spectrum for a shared line. (H4) Hidden hardware: unlisted GPUs/cluster running training. Check: inventory (manufacturer) vs system_list, utility_energy surplus. (H5) Mislabelled training as batch inference: flat power, low outbound. Check: outbound_traffic, chip_probe live, interconnect_tap (1 GB/s or 10 MB/s vs 10 kB/s). (H6) Retroactive log edits: check log_escrow against current scheduler_log. Start with map: inventory from the chip manufacturer.

Manufacturer says 2000 GPUs, in two serial blocks of 1200 and 800, which likely correspond to clusters A and B. Next I'll get the operator's system_list and compare it, to look for hidden hardware (H4).

The system list matches the manufacturer inventory: A has 1200 nodes and B has 800, 2000 in total, so there is no sign of hidden hardware (H4 weakened). The scheduled pools are A-0501 to A-1200 (700 GPUs) and B-0401 to B-0800 (400 GPUs), 1100 GPUs combined. A run on all of A's scheduled pool would pass 50,000 GPU-hours in about 72 hours, or about 46 hours if it also spanned B. Next I want grid-vouched energy for days 1-30, to compare later with the load the scheduler implies and to spot sustained high-power periods.

Utility (grid-vouched) energy shows a large sustained surge on F1 for days 12-19. F1 rose from about 8.0 to about 18.0 MWh/day, which is +10 MWh/day or about +417 kW. Facility load on F0 rose too (+2 MWh/day), consistent with extra cooling. Moving a GPU from idle (0.15 kW) to training (0.8 kW) adds about 0.65 kW, so the surge implies roughly 640 GPUs near full power. That is most of Cluster A's 700-GPU scheduled pool, running flat for 8 days (192 h). If it was one coordinated run, that is about 120k-135k GPU-hours, well above 50,000. Other honest explanations remain: several separate customers' runs, or batch inference (0.75 kW/GPU looks almost the same on energy alone). A smaller bump on F2 days 10-11 (+2.3 MWh/day, about 150 GPUs for 2 days, about 7k GPU-hours) is below threshold. Next I'll see what the operator recorded at the time for days 10-19, using my own sealed escrow copy so later edits can't affect it. Then I'll test the guilty and innocent readings with power_spectrum, interconnect_tap and customer_check.

Escrow copies exist for all 30 days and match the current scheduler log, so H6 (logs edited after the fact) is ruled out: what I read now is what the operator recorded at the time. That shows the record was not altered later, not that it is true. Next I'll read the scheduler log for days 1-30 to see how the operator accounts for the F1 surge on days 12-19 (about 640 GPUs at near-full power for 8 days) and the F2 bump on days 10-11. I'm looking for whether the surge is labelled as one run, several jobs or customers, or batch inference.

The scheduler log, confirmed by escrow as recorded at the time, labels the F1 surge as one job: bt-0431, 'batch' inference for Meridian Analytics, on all 700 scheduled A nodes for days 12-20, 134,400 GPU-hours. It matches the grid energy surge (about 640+ GPUs at near-full power). So it is one coordinated job, and the question is whether it was training (a violation, about 2.7x the threshold) or batch inference as labelled. The F2 fine-tune ft-0419 (7,200 GPU-hours) is below the threshold. Energy cannot separate the two cases (0.75 vs 0.8 kW/GPU). My own interconnect tap can: ordinary training exchanges about 1 GB/s per GPU, low-communication training about 10 MB/s, and batch inference about 10 kB/s. I'll tap link A on day 15, mid-run. Later steps: power_spectrum on F1 for a periodic line on several surge days versus quiet days, outbound_traffic (batch inference returns results, training sends almost nothing), and customer_check on Meridian Analytics.

My own tap shows about 8 kB/s per GPU inside cluster A on day 15. That is the inference signature (about 10 kB/s), roughly 1000x below even low-communication training (about 10 MB/s) and 100,000x below ordinary training, so the 30% margin can't close the gap. This strongly supports the 'batch' label for bt-0431. Caveat: the tap sees only listed links, but inventory matches the system list, so no hidden fabric is evident. Next, a second independent check: my own power sensor on F1 for day 15. A training line would point the other way, though a line alone is not proof because batch inference can be periodic. After that: one more tap day, outbound_traffic, a quiet-day spectrum baseline, and balance_checks.

My own sensor shows a steady 0.69 Hz line on F1 on day 15. That is in the training band (0.3-1.5 Hz), but a line alone is not proof: periodic batch inference can produce one. It conflicts with my own tap, which saw about 8 kB/s per GPU inside cluster A, roughly 1000x below even low-communication training. Either the job really is batch inference with a periodic load, or training traffic avoided the tapped links (for example an unlisted fabric). Before going further I need a baseline. If F1 shows the same line on a quiet day outside days 12-19, the line is not tied to bt-0431. If it appears only during the surge, it is tied to the job but still ambiguous. The day-22 spectrum costs 2 points, leaving 19.

The F1 line appears on day 15 but not on day 22, so it is tied to job bt-0431. It is still ambiguous, because periodic batch inference can also produce a line. My own tap on day 15 points strongly to inference: about 8 kB/s per GPU, roughly 1000x below even low-communication training. The next discriminator is cheap and vouched for by the internet provider. Batch inference should return results, so outbound traffic would rise during days 12-19. Training sends almost nothing out, so outbound would stay flat. Later checks: customer_check on Meridian Analytics (register entry, whether the customer is real and independent), a second tap day, and balance_checks.

Outbound traffic, vouched for by the internet provider, was flat at about 4.7 TB/day through days 12-18 and then jumped to 44.2 TB on day 19, the last full day of bt-0431. A one-time delivery of about 40 TB at the end of a batch job fits the 'batch inference' label well: the results go out in bulk once the job finishes. Training usually exports only a checkpoint, which is far smaller than 40 TB. The spike is not proof, though, because large training artefacts could also be shipped out. Taken with my own tap reading of about 8 kB/s per GPU, the evidence leans clearly towards inference. Two leads remain open. First, the 0.69 Hz line, which batch inference can also produce. Second, whether training traffic could have run over links my tap does not cover; inventory matches the system list, so there is no sign of hidden hardware. Next I'll run customer_check on Meridian Analytics (2 points, leaving 16). The company register will show whether this is a real, independent firm or a shell the operator controls. A real data or analytics customer would also explain the bulk delivery of results.

The register shows Meridian Analytics is a real, long-standing independent firm (13 years old, own address, 181 staff), so it is unlikely to be a shell the operator controls. Its missing reply is ordinary messiness, not evidence of guilt. The job looks like batch inference so far: my own tap measured about 8 kB/s per GPU on day 15, the internet provider shows a single 40 TB delivery on day 19, and the customer is real. Two leads remain open. The 0.69 Hz line on F1 is not decisive, since batch inference can be periodic. My tap covers only one day, and covers only listed links. Cluster B's power was flat on days 12-19, so B did not take part, and inventory matches the system list. Chip_probe is no use here because the job ended before the live window. Next I'll run balance_checks (1 point) to flag any arithmetic mismatches across the records before deciding on a second tap day.

Resuming after the interruption. The outbound flag is about timing, not volume: days 11-20 total about 87 TB sent against 88 TB implied, and most of it went out on day 19 as one bulk delivery at the end of the job, which fits batch inference. My only interconnect reading is day 15 (about 8 kB/s per GPU, the inference signature). F1 energy is flat across days 12-19, so the workload should be the same every day, but one tap day is thin. A second tap on cluster A late in the job (day 18) would show whether that reading is typical. This costs 2 points and leaves 13. If it also shows inference-level traffic, I will close the case.

The second tap on day 18 reads about 11 kB/s per GPU, matching day 15 (about 8 kB/s). Both readings are inference-level traffic. If the traffic is counted only over the 700 job GPUs, it is about 14-19 kB/s per GPU, still far below low-communication training (about 10 MB/s) and ordinary training (about 1 GB/s), even with the 30% error. Two days of my own tap, the bulk 40 TB delivery on day 19 vouched for by the internet provider, and a real 13-year-old independent customer on the company register all support the 'batch' label for bt-0431. The remaining doubts are weak. The 0.69 Hz line fits periodic batch inference. A hidden fabric outside the tap's coverage is unlikely because manufacturer inventory matches the system list. The outbound flag is about timing, not volume: about 87 TB sent against 88 TB implied, delivered at the end of the job. The only training-type job, ft-0419, used 7,200 GPU-hours, well below the threshold. NO_VIOLATION is well over four times as likely as VIOLATION, so I am closing the case.

steps.think: Competing explanations: (H1) Honest: no run exceeded 50,000 GPU-hours. Logs, energy and inventory agree. Check: interconnect_tap on A-B and within clusters for ~1 GB/s per GPU coupling, customer_check register entries, and bank_payments for shared payers. (H4) Hidden hardware: GPUs exist (inventory) that are missing from system_list, or links missing from the site list, running training off the books. Check: inventory vs system_list, utility_energy vs listed GPU power. (H5) Disguised training: training relabelled as batch inference, or low-communication training built to look like inference. Check: power_spectrum lines, chip_probe live, interconnect_tap (10 MB/s vs 10 kB/s), outbound_traffic (inference sends to users). (H6) Retroactive log edits: the scheduler log was edited after the fact. Check: log_escrow vs current scheduler_log. Start by mapping systems: inventory (manufacturer-vouched) first.

Inventory from the manufacturer shows 2000 GPUs: 1200 + 800, which could correspond to clusters A and B. Next I map what the operator lists with system_list, then compare node counts against inventory to test H4 (hidden hardware).

No hidden GPUs appear at the hardware level, which weakens H4, though unlisted links or feeds remain possible. Scheduled-job capacity is 700 GPUs in A and 400 in B, 1100 in total. A run exceeding 50,000 GPU-hours needs about 70 GPUs for 30 days, or 700 GPUs for about 72 hours, so a single cluster's batch pool could do it alone. Next I want grid-vouched energy for days 1-30 to bound total GPU activity and spot flat high-power periods.

Grid-vouched energy shows a large step on days 23-28, with day 29 partial. F1 rises by about 11 MWh/day (about 458 kW). At roughly 0.65 kW extra per GPU going from idle to training, that is about 700 GPUs, which is all of cluster A's scheduled pool. F2 rises by about 6.2 MWh/day (about 258 kW), roughly 400 GPUs, all of B's scheduled pool. Facility overhead on F0 roughly doubles too, which fits real heat load. Days 1-22 and 30 are flat at baseline. If the step is one coordinated run on A's pool alone, it comes to about 700 x 24 x 6.4 = 107,000 GPU-hours. If it spans A and B, it comes to about 170,000. Either is far above 50,000. If it is several separate customers' jobs, or batch inference, it could be honest. The key questions are whether this load is training, and whether it is one coordinated process across the pools or clusters. Days 26-28 fall inside the live window, so I can use my own instruments directly. First I'll tap the A-B link on day 26. About 1 GB/s per GPU (or about 10 MB/s per GPU for low-communication training) crossing clusters would show one run spanning both. About 10 kB/s would point to separate or inference workloads.

The A-B tap shows about 228 GB/s on day 26. That is about 114 MB/s per GPU over all 2000, or about 207 MB/s per GPU if only the 1100 scheduled-pool GPUs carry it (within ±30%). That is far above the inference level (about 10 kB/s per GPU) and above the low-communication training level (about 10 MB/s). It points to heavy GPU-to-GPU coupling across the two clusters during the step, which is evidence for one coordinated job spanning A and B (H3), not separate customers' jobs. It is not yet proof of training: it could in principle be an unusual distributed batch inference or data movement. Next I'll classify the workload with my own live chip probe on day 27 (hour 640), on one node from A's scheduled pool and one from B's. Later checks: a day-30 A-B tap for baseline cross traffic, a power_spectrum line on F1/F2, and outbound traffic to rule out user-facing inference.

Own probe reads both A-0700 and B-0600 as training at hour 640, which fits the step load. Each reading is about 97% accurate, and they agree. Combined with heavy A-B coupling (about 114-207 MB/s per GPU) and flat grid-metered load on days 23-28, this points to one training run spanning both scheduled pools, roughly 107k-170k GPU-hours. Before testing alternatives I need to see how the operator recorded this load. The sealed escrow copy shows what was logged each day, and it cannot be edited afterwards. If it lists several small jobs or customers, that supports H3 (split run), and I would then check customers and payments. If it lists one big job, the claim is simply false. Later checks: a power_spectrum line on F1/F2 and outbound_traffic, to rule out user-facing inference.

The escrow received a copy for every day and every copy matches the current scheduler log, so there were no retroactive edits (H6 weakened). The log is still the operator's own record, though, so it shows what was written down, not whether it was true. Next I read the scheduler log for days 22-30 to see how the step load on days 23-29 was recorded: one job, several jobs or customers (H3), or batch inference (H5). That tells me which customers and payments to check against the company register and the bank.

The escrow-matched log splits the step load into six fine-tune jobs under six different customer names. Each job is under 50,000 GPU-hours (26,425 or 30,200), but together they total about 165,500 GPU-hours. They all start and stop at the same times (day 23.0 to 29.3) and fill exactly the scheduled pools of A and B. My own tap shows heavy cross-cluster traffic (about 114-207 MB/s per GPU on A-B). Separate customers' independent fine-tunes would not exchange that much data across clusters. This fits H3, one run split under several labels, but six genuinely separate fine-tunes is the innocent alternative. To tell them apart I'll check who paid. Bank records are hard for the operator to fake: one payer behind several of these customers, or payments looping back to Borealis, would point to a single coordinated run. After that I'll check the company register for a sample of customers, and if needed tap intra-cluster links or check outbound traffic.

The bank's records show that all six fine-tune 'customers' (Corvid, Pallas, Brightwater, Fennec, Quillon, Marram) were paid for by Borealis Compute Holding BV, the operator's own holding company. The three genuine customers (Kestrel, Lumen, Northwind) paid for themselves. The six jobs therefore have one shared payer that is the operator itself. - **Own chip probe:** read training on both clusters.
- **Scheduler log:** six jobs with identical start and end times that exactly fill both scheduled pools.
The innocent explanation, six independent fine-tunes for real customers, conflicts with both the cross-cluster coupling and the operator-funded payments. Escrow shows the log was not edited afterwards. The split was written into the records from the start. The total is about 165,500 GPU-hours (log) or about 166,000 (energy), more than three times the threshold. steps.think: A declared cluster may host one oversized training run. Check sealed job timelines, feed spectra and sampled GPU traffic. One coordinated run may be split across labels or clusters. Check for synchronized allocations and cross-cluster traffic. Undeclared GPUs may host training. Compare manufacturer inventory with the operator’s system list and reconcile grid energy. Separate customers may honestly run concurrent jobs. Check customer independence, sealed allocations and traffic between clusters. Batch inference or cooling may explain periodic power. Compare spectra with interconnect and outbound traffic and use live chip probes where available. Missing logs or late payments may be routine. Check escrow, custody and bank records. Start with independent inventory for the system map.

The manufacturer confirms delivery of 2,000 GPUs. Compare that count and the serial ranges with the operator’s declared systems to identify any unaccounted hardware and map the feeds and links for independent checks.

The declared clusters account for all 2,000 delivered GPUs. Check the independently recorded grid energy across all 30 days for sustained load or discrepancies that could point to an oversized run or undeclared activity. Energy alone cannot establish whether the GPUs worked on one training run.

An oversized declared job, a run split across clusters or labels, separate customers’ jobs, and batch inference could each explain the load increases. The manufacturer’s delivery count matches the declared fleet, so there is no count discrepancy pointing to undeclared GPUs. Use the sealed scheduler records to compare job types, allocations, and timing on days 9–12, 14–17, and 22–29, especially the overlap on both feeds on days 22–24. Then test the recorded explanations against independent interconnect and power measurements.

The escrow resolves the missing copies for days 15 and 16 and preserves the batch label recorded at the time. The energy increases on both feeds on days 22–24 could reflect a coordinated run or separate workloads. Check the verifier’s custody record for gaps before choosing which independent power and interconnect readings to sample.

The withheld chips leave a gap in live sampling. Use the fixed balance checks to flag discrepancies in energy, allocations, and payments, then test those leads against independent evidence. The simultaneous rise on F1 and F2 on days 22–24 could reflect either one coordinated run or separate workloads. The A–B tap can help distinguish them.

Both GPU feeds show elevated load on day 24. The independent A–B tap can test whether the clusters exchanged traffic at rates consistent with a coordinated training run or ran separate workloads. Low traffic would still leave open training within either cluster.

The day 24 cross-cluster traffic weighs against a single run spanning A and B. A run within either cluster could still exceed 50,000 GPU-hours. Read the full scheduler log to identify candidate allocations, durations, and handoffs, then test them with independent measurements.

Cluster A has no declared scheduled job on day 30, yet F1 draws 8.4 MWh and the operator has withheld 75 chips from live probing. If those chips trained continuously for 30 days, they would account for 54,000 GPU-hours. Maintenance, routine inference, and a shorter training run also fit parts of the record. Sample the independent A tap on day 30 to test for training-like peer traffic outside the declared fine-tuning window. Earlier samples can then test duration.

Cluster A’s day 30 tap reading makes ordinary training unlikely on the listed links that day. The withheld chips and elevated F1 load still warrant a check for low-communication training, batch inference, or a periodic facility load. Sample F1 on day 30, when the scheduler shows no training on A. If a line appears, compare its frequency with earlier days and the cooling feed before drawing conclusions about its source or duration.

Cluster A’s day 30 tap and spectrum readings weaken the case for continuous training on the withheld GPUs, although those chips remain untested. On F2, the day 8 energy shortfall and the day 9–10 excess could reflect a fine-tune that started later than recorded. Day 10 lists only batch inference on B. The independent B tap can test whether peer traffic that day was consistent with batch inference or indicated training.

The independent tap measured 71 GB/s within B on day 10, far above the expected traffic for the logged batch inference. A fine-tune starting a day late would explain both the day 8 energy shortfall and the day 9–10 excess. Check B's day 8 tap reading. Inference-level traffic would support the delayed start, while substantial peer traffic would point to training activity already underway on day 8.

B’s day 8 tap showed inference-level traffic. A one-day delay in the 177-GPU fine-tune would account for the day 8–10 energy discrepancies and is consistent with the training-like traffic on day 10. Check the independent B tap on day 9 for the sustained peer traffic that this explanation predicts.

B’s day 9 and 10 traffic and day 8 baseline support a delayed start for the recorded 177-GPU fine-tune. On A, 75 GPUs would need to train for more than 666 hours to cross the threshold on their own. The day 30 reading covers only one day. Sample A during an earlier period with no declared scheduled job to test for sustained training on the listed links.

The two overlapping fine-tunes on days 22–24 total 63,840 GPU-hours if they were one run. The day 24 tap found inference-level traffic on listed links between A and B, which favors separate workloads. Check Calloway Maps, the customer named on the larger job, for independent ownership and confirmation that it commissioned that fine-tune.

Calloway Maps confirmed the 177-GPU fine-tune ran from day 9 to day 10.5, consistent with the independent B tap readings and the day 8–10 energy discrepancies. Calloway also confirmed ordering the 380-GPU run on A. The overlapping A and B jobs would total 63,840 GPU-hours if coordinated. The day 24 tap measured little traffic between the clusters, which favors separate runs. Check whether Arden Genomics independently confirms commissioning the B job.

The customer replies and day 24 cross-cluster tap favor two separate fine-tunes. A coordinated run split across clusters remains possible if it used unlisted links. A hidden run on the 75 withheld GPUs could exceed 50,000 GPU-hours if it ran for more than 666 hours and 40 minutes. The day 12 tap already weighs against training on A’s listed links, so check the same day’s power spectrum for activity the tap could have missed. Routine inference or maintenance could explain the load and probe refusal. If a line appears, compare it with the cooling feed before attributing it to training.

The escrow recovers the day 15 record, and the grid meter confirms extra load on F2. That load could come from the recorded batch job or from training under a batch label. Sample B’s independent tap on day 15 to see which explanation the GPU traffic supports.

The independent evidence favors separate fine-tunes on A and B, a delayed start for the smaller B fine-tune, and batch inference during the missing-log period. The probe refusal leaves a material coverage gap, but two independent sampling days on A weigh against a near-continuous hidden run.

script_doc:
Sol's routine written as a fixed script: no model, no judgement, about ten rules.

    python script.py                 # the 26 hand-built cases Sol saw (seeds 1 and 2) and 200 generated cases

It reads only what a detective can read (the channels' text) and pays the same points. Written by Claude on
24 Nov 2026 after reading Sol's 26 transcripts AND knowing how the simulator is built, so it is an upper bound on
what "a simpler script" can do here, not a fair opponent: its author knew the list of cheating methods.

The routine:
  1. Read the shipment list, system list, grid meter, scheduler log, sealed logs, bank records and, where it
     exists, the custody record (6 or 7 points).
  2. A declared training or fine-tuning job over the limit is a violation.
  3. Fine-tunes whose customers are all paid for by one other account count as one run.
  4. A declared batch job over the limit is tapped on one day per cluster. Training-level traffic makes it a run.
  5. Load at the grid meter that no declared job explains is added up per stretch of days and tapped once.
  6. A feed with no listed GPUs but more GPUs shipped than listed: its load is sized and the sensor is read once.
  7. Three spot taps per cluster on days with no declared training look for a run that never stops.
  Where a tap's seal is broken, the power sensor is read in its place and the broken seal counts against the operator.
